words.definition: Persistent, careful attention and hard work devoted to a task over time.
words.example: Her assiduity at the lab bench, arriving before dawn every day, impressed the senior researchers.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a SIT DUTY' — you sit down and do your duty without ever quitting.

words.definition: Showing dedicated, careful, and persistent effort in one's work.
words.example: The sedulous apprentice polished every joint until the finished cabinet was flawless.
words.mnemonic: 'SED-you-lose' — the worker acts as if they were told they'd lose unless every detail is done.

words.definition: The quality of working hard with steady, attentive care.
words.example: Years of quiet sedulity turned his failing corner shop into a thriving business.
words.mnemonic: The noun form of 'sedulous': picture a steady bee that 'said you' must keep going.

words.definition: Able to keep going without ever becoming tired or giving up.
words.example: The indefatigable volunteer sorted donations for sixteen hours and still asked for more boxes.
words.mnemonic: Break it up: in- (not) + 'fatigue' + -able — literally 'not able to be fatigued.'

words.definition: Working hard in a steady and productive way.
words.example: The industrious student filled three notebooks before the semester had even begun.
words.mnemonic: Think of a busy 'industry' full of workers — industrious people hum along like a factory.

words.definition: Careful, steady, and thorough in doing one's work.
words.example: A diligent accountant, she checked every figure twice before filing the report.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'do it, gent' — a gentleman who does the job properly and fully.

words.definition: Careful and persistent effort put into a task.
words.example: His diligence in researching the case uncovered a detail everyone else had missed.
words.mnemonic: Think 'due diligence' — the careful checking a buyer does before closing a deal.

words.definition: Continuing steadily without any pause or easing off.
words.example: The unremitting rain battered the coast for nine straight days.
words.mnemonic: un- + 'remit' (to let up or ease) — so it never lets up.

words.definition: Staying strong and steady without weakening or tiring.
words.example: Her unflagging enthusiasm kept the team moving through the final grueling mile.
words.mnemonic: un- + 'flagging' (drooping like a limp flag) — a banner that never sags.

words.definition: A fine or precise point of formal conduct, etiquette, or procedure.
words.example: The diplomat observed every punctilio, bowing at the exact angle protocol demanded.
words.mnemonic: Shares its Latin root (punctum, 'point') with 'punctual' and 'point' — a tiny point of correctness.

words.definition: Done with great care, attention, and thoroughness.
words.example: After painstaking restoration, every cracked tile in the mosaic looked brand new.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'taking pains' — going to great trouble to get every detail right.

words.definition: Requiring a lot of hard, tiring work or effort.
words.example: Translating the ancient text was laborious, costing her a decade of late nights.
words.mnemonic: It contains 'labor' — something full of labor, heavy work.

words.definition: Very difficult and demanding great physical or mental effort.
words.example: The arduous climb up the icy ridge left even seasoned guides gasping.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'hard-uous' — an arduous task is just plain hard.

words.definition: Involving a heavy, burdensome load of duty or difficulty.
words.example: The new regulations placed onerous paperwork on every small farm owner.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'onus' (a burden) — an onerous duty sits on you like a weight.

words.definition: Marked by long, tiring, and difficult work.
words.example: The toilsome harvest stretched from sunrise to dark, bending every back in the village.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'toil' (hard labor) plus -some — something full of toil.

words.definition: Requiring or using a lot of physical or mental energy and hard work.
words.example: The climb up the north face was so strenuous that even the seasoned guides paused to catch their breath.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'strain' + 'us' — activities that strain us and leave us worn out.

words.definition: Involving or requiring a great deal of tedious effort and hard work.
words.example: Restoring the manuscript letter by letter proved an operose undertaking that consumed three full years.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'opus/opera' means work — 'operose' is something full of work.

words.definition: Concerned with dull, mechanical, or purely practical matters rather than culture or ideas.
words.example: He dismissed bookkeeping as banausic labor, beneath a poet of his supposed gifts.
words.mnemonic: Think 'banal' — banal + mechanical; from Greek 'banausos', a mere artisan or mechanic.

words.definition: Hard, menial, and dull work that feels boring and unrewarding.
words.example: After a decade of factory drudgery, she longed for a job that finally engaged her mind.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dredge' + 'grungy' — dredging up grungy, dreary chores.

words.definition: A person made to do hard, dull, or menial tasks.
words.example: In the counting-house he was little more than a drudge, copying ledgers from dawn to dusk.
words.mnemonic: Picture a weary worker 'trudging' through endless chores — a drudge trudges.

words.definition: To work very hard, often at wet, dirty, or exhausting labor.
words.example: They moiled in the flooded mines from morning till night for a pittance.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'toil' and 'soil' — hard toil down in the soil.

words.definition: To work extremely hard for a long time, usually at exhausting tasks.
words.example: Farmers toiled under the blazing sun to bring in the harvest before the storm hit.
words.mnemonic: Hear the 'oil' of sweat glistening on a laborer's brow — toil.

words.definition: The use of considerable physical or mental effort and energy.
words.example: After the exertion of hauling crates all afternoon, his arms trembled uncontrollably.
words.mnemonic: From 'exert' — to push force out; exertion is the outward push of energy.

words.definition: Stubborn and unyielding determination to hold to a purpose or opinion.
words.example: She pursued the appeal with such pertinacity that the court finally agreed to rehear the case.
words.mnemonic: 'Per-' (through) + 'tenacity' — a pit bull that pushes through and won't let go.

words.definition: Careful, thorough, and guided by a strong sense of duty in one's work.
words.example: A conscientious editor, she checked every citation twice before the book went to print.
words.mnemonic: It literally contains 'conscience' — a conscientious person listens to their conscience.

words.definition: Extremely thorough, careful, and strict in method or standards.
words.example: The vaccine passed a rigorous series of trials before regulators would approve it.
words.mnemonic: 'Rigor' evokes 'rigid' — rigorous standards are stiff and unbending.

words.definition: Making great demands on one's skill, attention, care, or effort.
words.example: The jeweler's exacting standards meant a single flaw sent the whole batch back.
words.mnemonic: From 'exact' — an exacting boss wants everything precise and exact.

words.definition: A long spell of hard, tedious work, or a difficult, laborious walk.
words.example: Writing the dissertation was a two-year slog through mountains of raw data.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'slow' + 'jog' through mud — heavy, plodding, wearying effort.

words.definition: A paid position that requires little or no actual work or responsibility.
words.example: The honorary chairmanship was a sinecure: a title, a salary, and almost nothing to do.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'sine cura' = 'without care' — a job that comes with no cares or duties.

words.definition: An employee who handles many different kinds of tasks and duties.
words.example: As the studio's factotum, he answered phones, fixed the lights, and even edited scripts.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'fac totum' = 'do everything' — a factotum does the total of all jobs.

words.definition: A person who works only for payment, showing little loyalty or care for the cause.
words.example: The mercenary captain was a hireling who would switch sides the moment a richer lord waved his purse.
words.mnemonic: "Hire" + "-ling": a little person you HIRE for cash — loyal to the coin, not the cause.

words.definition: A skilled worker who makes quality goods by hand.
words.example: Each loaf was shaped by an artisan who had spent decades mastering the craft.
words.mnemonic: ART + -isan — one who makes ART-like, handcrafted things.

words.definition: A trained worker who is competent and reliable but not yet a master.
words.example: He's no star, but as a steady journeyman he has served eight clubs over fifteen dependable seasons.
words.mnemonic: From French 'journée' (a day) — once a worker paid by the day, past apprenticeship but short of master.

words.definition: The social class of low-paid workers who own no means of production.
words.example: Marx argued that the proletariat, owning only their labor, would one day rise against the factory owners.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'proles' (offspring) — the lowest Roman class whose only asset was their children and labor.

words.definition: Relating to the class of low-paid workers who own no property.
words.example: The novel captured proletarian life: cramped tenements, factory whistles, and pay gone by week's end.
words.mnemonic: 'Prole' + '-arian' (of a type, like 'vegetarian') — of the working type.

words.definition: A feudal system in which laborers are legally bound to land and its owner.
words.example: Freed from serfdom, the peasants could finally leave the estate and seek work in the towns.
words.mnemonic: 'Serf' sounds like 'surf' — but a serf could never surf away; he was chained to the lord's land.

words.definition: The entire collection of creative works produced by one artist over a lifetime.
words.example: Critics reviewing her oeuvre traced how her paintings evolved across four decades.
words.mnemonic: French for 'work' (say 'OO-vruh') — picture a whole hors d'oeuvre spread of an artist's output.

words.definition: Dull, ordinary, and lacking any variety or excitement.
words.example: After the thrill of travel, returning to her humdrum office routine felt unbearably grey.
words.mnemonic: The monotonous HUM of a DRUM beating the same flat note over and over.

words.definition: Mundane and practical, belonging to the ordinary routine of normal life.
words.example: She traded her glamorous stage costumes for the workaday clothes of a schoolteacher.
words.mnemonic: Break it up: 'work-a-day' — just another plain day of toil, nothing special.

words.definition: Carefully watchful and alert to possible danger or trouble.
words.example: The lifeguard stayed vigilant, scanning the waves for any swimmer in distress.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'vigil' (awake watch) — a vigilant person keeps a vigil, staying awake to watch.

words.definition: Careful, continuous attention aimed at detecting possible danger or trouble.
words.example: Constant vigilance at the border checkpoint meant no smuggler slipped through unnoticed.
words.mnemonic: Same 'vigil' root as staying awake — keeping an unbroken wakeful watch.

words.definition: Lively, energetic, and full of cheerful movement.
words.example: At ninety, she was still sprightly enough to dance a jig at the party.
words.mnemonic: 'Sprite' + '-ly' — bouncing about like a quick, lively little sprite.

words.definition: Hearty enthusiasm and evident enjoyment in doing something.
words.example: He attacked the enormous plate of pasta with such gusto that everyone laughed.
words.mnemonic: Italian 'gusto' = taste — you 'taste' life fully; a gusty gale of relish.

words.definition: The quality of energetic force and constant activity that drives progress.
words.example: The startup's dynamism was infectious: new ideas, rapid launches, and a team that never stood still.
words.mnemonic: Root 'dynamo' — a dynamo generates power; this is that generating energy in action.

words.definition: A driving force or motivation that makes something happen or advance.
words.example: The scandal gave fresh impetus to demands for reform across the police force.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'impact' / 'impetuous' — a push that impacts and sets things moving.

words.definition: Acting or carried out with speed and efficiency.
words.example: The courier promised expeditious delivery, and the package arrived within the hour.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'expedite' crossed with 'ambitious' — you expedite a task with ambitious speed.

words.definition: Intense warmth of feeling, passion, or zeal.
words.example: She pursued her research with such ardor that she often forgot to eat.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ardere,' to burn — ardor is a feeling that burns hot like embers.

words.definition: A habitual love of ease and a dislike of work or effort.
words.example: Weeks of indolence left his garden overgrown and his projects untouched.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + sounds like 'doldrums' — no drive, just drifting in lazy doldrums.

words.definition: Reluctant to work or exert oneself; marked by laziness.
words.example: The slothful clerk let a month of paperwork pile up untouched.
words.mnemonic: Picture the animal sloth hanging motionless in a tree all day long.

words.definition: Serving no useful purpose; pointless or ineffective.
words.example: Once the contract was signed, further negotiation seemed otiose.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'otium' (leisure); say 'oh-tee-ohs' — so idle it does nothing worthwhile.

words.definition: A state of stillness, inactivity, or temporary rest.
words.example: After the eruption, the volcano entered a long period of quiescence.
words.mnemonic: 'Quiet' + 'essence' — the very essence of being quiet and still.

words.definition: A state of drowsiness or a strong desire to sleep.
words.example: The warm room and the droning lecture brought on a heavy somnolence.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'somnus' means sleep (as in insomnia) — somnolence is being full of sleep.

words.definition: A person who is habitually lazy and avoids work.
words.example: Get up, you sluggard — the others finished their chores hours ago!
words.mnemonic: 'Slug' + '-ard' — a person who creeps along as slowly as a garden slug.

words.definition: A person who moves or responds more slowly than others.
words.example: The laggard at the back of the group kept the whole hike waiting.
words.mnemonic: 'Lag' + '-ard' — one who lags behind everyone else.

words.definition: To waste time or move aimlessly slowly while doing something.
words.example: Stop dawdling over breakfast or we'll miss the train.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'doodle' — doodling around instead of getting anything done.

words.definition: To stand or wait around idly without any clear purpose.
words.example: Teenagers would loiter outside the shop for hours every evening.
words.mnemonic: Think of the 'No Loitering' sign — picture people hanging around aimlessly beneath it.

words.definition: Someone who pretends to be ill to escape duty or work.
words.example: The sergeant suspected the soldier was a malingerer feigning a limp before drills.
words.mnemonic: 'Mal' (bad) + 'linger' — you linger in bed claiming a bad illness to dodge duty.

words.definition: To deliberately avoid or neglect a responsibility or duty.
words.example: He would never shirk his share of the cleanup, however unpleasant it got.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'work' but means to dodge it — 'shirk the work.'

words.definition: A person who habitually avoids work or responsibility.
words.example: No shirker lasted long on a crew that depended on every hand.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'worker' but is its opposite — the one who ducks the job.

words.definition: A person who spends time doing nothing or avoiding work.
words.example: The park bench was a favorite perch for the town's idlers.
words.mnemonic: An engine at 'idle' runs but goes nowhere — neither does this person.

words.definition: A person who avoids work and passes the time doing nothing useful.
words.example: While his roommates job-hunted, the loafer stayed on the couch playing games until noon.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'loaf' — picture someone lying around like a lazy loaf of bread all day.

words.definition: Showing no enthusiasm, effort, or determination; carelessly casual.
words.example: Her lackadaisical shrug told the coach she didn't care whether the team won or lost.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'lack-a-daisy' — too listless even to bend down and pick a daisy.

words.definition: Showing no interest, emotion, or concern about anything.
words.example: Voters were so apathetic that barely a fifth of them bothered to show up at the polls.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'a-' (without) + 'pathos' (feeling) = without feeling.

words.definition: Failing to give the proper care or attention that a situation requires.
words.example: The negligent babysitter scrolled her phone while the toddler wandered toward the pool.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'neglect-gent' — a gentleman who neglects everything he's responsible for.

words.definition: Failure to take the care that a responsible person normally would.
words.example: The bridge collapsed, and investigators blamed years of maintenance negligence by the city.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'neg-' (not) + 'legere' (to pick up) — not picking up your responsibilities.

words.definition: The quality of being insufficiently strict, firm, or careful.
words.example: The bank's laxity about verifying identities let the fraudsters open dozens of fake accounts.
words.mnemonic: 'Lax' sounds like 'slacks' — loose pants stand for loose, sloppy standards.

words.definition: To reduce in speed, tension, or intensity.
words.example: As the storm passed, the wind began to slacken and the sails hung limp.
words.mnemonic: 'Slack' + '-en' — to make slack, the way a rope goes loose when you stop pulling.

words.definition: Lacking purpose, competence, or the will to accomplish anything.
words.example: Her feckless brother lost three jobs in a year and never once paid his share of rent.
words.mnemonic: 'Feck' is old Scots for 'effect' or 'worth' — so feckless means without effect.

words.definition: Lacking ambition, energy, or the drive to improve oneself.
words.example: The foreman fired the shiftless crew who leaned on their shovels all afternoon.
words.mnemonic: 'Shift-less' — unwilling to shift (move) a single muscle to get ahead.

words.definition: A good-for-nothing person who squanders money, time, or opportunity.
words.example: The wastrel burned through his inheritance on cards and champagne within two years.
words.mnemonic: 'Waste' + '-rel' (as in scoundrel) — a scoundrel who wastes everything he touches.

words.definition: A state of mental dullness, sluggishness, and lethargy.
words.example: After the heavy lunch a thick hebetude settled over the office, and no one could think straight.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'he be dude' — a dude too dazed and dull to lift a finger.

words.definition: Spiritual or mental listlessness and lack of care about one's duties.
words.example: A gray acedia gripped the monk, who could no longer bring himself to pray or read.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'a-kedos' — without care; the 'noonday demon' that drained listless monks.

words.definition: Involving much sitting and little physical movement or exercise.
words.example: Years of a sedentary desk job left him stiff, soft, and short of breath on the stairs.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'sedere' (to sit) — same root as 'sedan' and 'sediment' that settles and sits.

words.definition: Going beyond what duty requires; more than is strictly necessary.
words.example: Staying late to mentor the new hire was supererogatory — kind, but nothing his contract demanded.
words.mnemonic: 'Super-' (above) + 'erogate' (to pay out) — paying out above and beyond the call.

words.definition: Exhaustion or emptiness caused by a lack of food or vitality.
words.example: Rescuers found the shipwrecked sailor near inanition, too weak from hunger to stand.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'inane' — Latin 'inanis' (empty); an utterly emptied, drained state.

words.definition: To work steadily at a trade, or to keep supplying someone with something insistently.
words.example: The old ferryman would ply the river between the two villages from dawn until dusk each day.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'apply' with the front chopped off — you apply yourself, working diligently at your craft.

words.definition: To search deeply and thoroughly for information about something.
words.example: Curious about her grandmother's past, she began to delve into old letters stored in the attic.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'shelve' — picture pulling every book off the shelf to dig deep for one buried fact.

description: advanced and low-frequency — labour and idleness
